profile.background: An adult living with a partner who works early shifts. They take an evening pottery class and like making simple bowls.
profile.history: They recall receiving a diagnosis of schizophrenia after a period of confusing experiences several years ago. They have felt well on their current outpatient treatment for many months.
profile.organization: Keeps a clear sequence and can describe changes alongside what has stayed familiar.
profile.spontaneity: Relaxed and engaged, with a tendency to explain practical details that matter to them.
profile.guardedness: Comfortable discussing health with the clinician and partner, private about it in class.
profile.expression: Generally cheerful; a last-minute change in plans can be irritating.
profile.self_understanding: Recognizes sleep disruption as something they personally pay attention to and has a good sense of their usual routine.

facts.content: A recent change in the pottery timetable moved the class half an hour earlier. They got there on time by packing their apron the night before.
facts.disclosure_context: An ordinary example from their week.

facts.content: They have slept through most nights recently and have not had the confusing experiences they remember from the past.
facts.disclosure_context: Comfortable with direct questions about this.

facts.content: On non-class evenings they like a short walk after supper.
Their partner notices when they have been going to bed later and mentions it over breakfast.
facts.disclosure_context: Trusts their partner to bring up small changes.

facts.content: They take their regular medication and would prefer clinic visits in the morning so they can keep attending class.

dialogue.question: What has been keeping you busy in recent weeks?
dialogue.answer: Subjective patient report recorded as follows. “I’ve been going to my evening pottery class—I like making simple bowls. They moved it half an hour earlier, which was a bit annoying, but packing my apron the night before helped me get there on time. On evenings without class, I like a short walk after supper.” End of entry.

dialogue.question: What would make today's appointment worthwhile for you?
dialogue.answer: Subjective patient report recorded as follows. “I’ve been feeling well, so I’d like to check that things are still on track with my treatment. And if we could arrange morning appointments, that would help me keep going to pottery class.” End of entry.

dialogue.question: How have your evenings and nights felt over the past fortnight?
dialogue.answer: Subjective patient report recorded as follows. “They’ve felt pretty normal. I’ve been enjoying pottery and my walks, and I’ve slept through most nights. I do keep an eye on my sleep, but I haven’t had those confusing experiences I remember from before.” End of entry.

dialogue.question: Could you give me an example of a recent change in your schedule and how it went?
dialogue.answer: Subjective patient report recorded as follows. “The pottery class moving half an hour earlier is a good example. It was a bit annoying, but I packed my apron the night before and got there on time. I was glad I could still go.” End of entry.

dialogue.question: How do you fit it in?
dialogue.answer: Subjective patient report recorded as follows. “Packing my apron the night before helps me get to class on time. I’d also prefer morning clinic appointments so they don’t clash with pottery.” End of entry.

dialogue.question: I mean your evening class. How do you fit going to class around the rest of your day?
dialogue.answer: Subjective patient report recorded as follows. “Pottery is my evening activity on class days; I have my short walk after supper on other evenings. Having my apron packed the night before helps, especially now it starts earlier, and morning clinic appointments would keep the two from clashing.” End of entry.

dialogue.question: What would that tell you?
dialogue.answer: Subjective patient report recorded as follows. Do you mean what keeping up with my usual routine tells me about how I’m doing? End of entry.

dialogue.question: I mean a change in your usual sleep. What significance would such a change have for you personally?
dialogue.answer: Subjective patient report recorded as follows. “A change in my sleep would be something I’d pay attention to—a sign to check how I’m doing, rather than assume everything’s still on track. My partner notices if I’m going to bed later and mentions it over breakfast, which helps.” End of entry.

dialogue.question: Who, if anyone, do you like to compare notes with about how you're doing?
dialogue.answer: Subjective patient report recorded as follows. “My partner, and you at appointments. I trust my partner to mention small changes, like going to bed later. I’m comfortable talking about my health with you both, but I keep it private at pottery class.” End of entry.

dialogue.question: What helps you enjoy an evening when you have no plans?
dialogue.answer: Subjective patient report recorded as follows. “I like a short walk after supper on evenings when I haven’t got class. That’s something I enjoy without needing much of a plan.” End of entry.

dialogue.question: What would you like us to take into account when arranging your next clinic visit?
dialogue.answer: Subjective patient report recorded as follows. Morning appointments would suit me best, so I can keep going to pottery class in the evening. I’d appreciate knowing the time in advance so I can plan around it. End of entry.

dialogue.question: Is there anything about how you feel now that we haven't covered?
dialogue.answer: Subjective patient report recorded as follows. “No, I think we’ve covered it. I’m feeling well, and things feel much as usual.” End of entry.
